en: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.1 The Chapter on Forms, etc. (Rūpādivagga) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates subject to clinging. [This concludes] the first discourse in the Chapter on Forms, etc., in the First Book of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [he said].
“Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Monks, I do not see even a single other form that so obsesses the mind of a man as the form of a woman does, monks.
The form of a woman, monks, obsesses the mind of a man. Thus was the first [discourse].

The sound of a woman, monks, obsesses a man’s mind.”

“Monks, there are these five hindrances: sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. Monks, there are these five factors of striving: the wish to abandon unarisen sensual desire, the wish to abandon arisen sensual desire; the wish to abandon unarisen ill will, the wish to abandon arisen ill will; the wish to abandon unarisen dullness and drowsiness, the wish to abandon arisen dullness and drowsiness; the wish to abandon unarisen restlessness and remorse, the wish to abandon arisen restlessness and remorse;

and the wish to abandon unarisen doubt, the wish to abandon arisen doubt. Monks, for one whose mind is sluggish, unarisen dullness and drowsiness arise, and arisen dullness and drowsiness lead to their increase and expansion. Thus was the third [sutta].
“Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single thing by which unarisen restlessness and remorse arise,
or by which arisen restlessness and remorse increase and expand,
as does the lack of tranquility of the mind.
“Monks, for one whose mind is unpacified, restlessness and remorse that have not yet arisen do arise, and restlessness and remorse that have already arisen lead to their increase and expansion.
This is the fourth.
“Monks, I do not see even a single other thing by which unarisen doubt... [does not arise].”
“Doubt that has not yet arisen arises, or doubt that has already arisen leads to its increase and expansion, namely, through improper attention, monks.
For one who attends improperly, monks, both unarisen doubt arises and arisen doubt leads to its increase and expansion.
Thus ends the fifth [sutta].
“Monks, I do not see even a single thing by which unarisen sensual desire does not arise, or by which arisen sensual desire is abandoned, as much as this, monks: the sign of the unattractive.
For one who attends thoroughly to the sign of the unattractive, monks, unarisen sensual desire does not arise, and arisen sensual desire is abandoned.”

For one who has aroused energy, monks, unarisen sloth and torpor do not arise, and arisen sloth and torpor are abandoned.”

“Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single thing by which, when unarisen, restlessness and remorse do not arise, or by which, when arisen, restlessness and remorse are abandoned, as much as this: the tranquility of the mind.
For one whose mind is tranquil, bhikkhus, unarisen restlessness and remorse do not arise, and arisen restlessness and remorse are abandoned.”

“Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single thing by which unarisen doubt does not arise, or by which arisen doubt is abandoned, as much as wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
For one who attends wisely, bhikkhus, unarisen doubt does not arise and arisen doubt is abandoned.”

The mind, bhikkhus, when developed, leads to great benefit.

The mind, bhikkhus, when developed and made manifest, leads to great benefit.

The mind, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, leads to great benefit.
(The eighth.)
“Monks, I do not see even a single other thing that, when undeveloped and uncultivated, brings such suffering as this: the mind, monks.
The mind, monks, when undeveloped and uncultivated, brings suffering. Thus ends the ninth [sutta].
“Monks, I do not see even a single other thing that, when developed and cultivated, brings such happiness as the mind.
Monks, the mind, when developed and cultivated, brings happiness.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.41 The Chapter on the Directed Mind (Paṇihitacitta-vagga) “Monks, there are these five persons found existing in the world. What five? The person who is directed toward the inferior; the person who is directed toward the superior; the person who has entered the stream;

the person who is a once-returner; and the person who is a non-returner. And how, monks, is one a person directed toward the inferior? Here, monks, someone is endowed with faith, yet he does not possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He is endowed with virtue, yet he does not possess unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He is endowed with generosity, yet he does not possess unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He is endowed with learning, yet he does not possess unwavering confidence in the training thus: ‘The trainings proclaimed by the Blessed One are well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to self-awakening, and properly expounded by the one who is truly awakened. This, monks, is called a person directed toward the inferior. And how, monks, is one a person directed toward the superior? Here, monks, someone is endowed with faith... endowed with virtue... endowed with generosity... endowed with learning, and he possesses unwavering confidence in the training thus: ‘The trainings proclaimed by the Blessed One are well-proclaimed... This, monks, is called a person directed toward the superior. And how, monks, is one a person who has entered the stream? Here, monks, someone is endowed with faith... endowed with virtue... endowed with generosity... endowed with learning, and he possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One... This, monks, is called a person who has entered the stream. And how, monks, is one a person who is a once-returner? Here, monks, someone is endowed with faith... endowed with virtue... endowed with generosity... endowed with learning, and he possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples... This, monks, is called a person who is a once-returner. And how, monks, is one a person who is a non-returner? Here, monks, someone is endowed with faith... endowed with virtue... endowed with generosity... endowed with learning, and he possesses unwavering confidence in the training thus: ‘The trainings proclaimed by the Blessed One are well-proclaimed... This, monks, is called a person who is a non-returner. These, monks, are the five persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, just as it is impossible for a grain of rice or a stalk of barley that has been wrongly directed, when stepped on by hand or foot, to break the hand or foot or draw blood— why is that?

“Here, monks, having encompassed with my own mind the mind of a certain person whose heart is corrupted, I understand:
‘If this person were to die at this very moment, he would be placed in hell as if carried there.’”
"And for what reason?
Because his mind, monks, is corrupted.

It is through the cause of mental corruption, monks, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell."

having encompassed with my own mind the mind of a certain person whose heart is full of confidence, I understand it thus:”

"But it is because of serenity of mind, bhikkhus, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.

“Monks, it is just as if there were a pool of water that was turbid, stirred up, and muddy;
a man with good eyesight standing on the bank would not see the shells and snails, the pebbles and gravel, or even schools of fish moving about or staying still. And why is that?
“Because of the turbidity of the water, monks.
Even so, monks, that bhikkhu with a turbid mind will surely not know his own welfare, nor know the welfare of others, nor know the welfare of both;
nor will he attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.”
"It is impossible that he will realize it.
And why is that? Because, monks, his mind is turbid."
The Fifth.

(AN 1.46, AN 1.5.6, PTS AN i 9) “Bhikkhus, just as if there were a pool of water that was clear, serene, and undisturbed, and a man with good sight standing on the bank could see shells, gravel, and pebbles, and also schools of fish moving about or staying still; even so...”
For what reason?
Because of the clarity of the water, monks.
In the same way, monks, that bhikkhu with an untroubled mind will indeed know his own welfare or the welfare of others.

It is possible that he will know both [the past and the future], or that he will know what lies beyond, or that he will realize a superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
For what reason?
“Because of the non-turbidity of the mind, monks,” [he said].

The mind, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, becomes supple and workable.”

“Bhikkhus, this mind is luminous.”

The uninstructed worldling does not understand this as it really is.
Therefore, I say that for the uninstructed worldling there is no development of the mind."

“Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who explain what is not an offense as an offense act for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many beings, including devas and humans. Furthermore, bhikkhus,
those bhikkhus generate much demerit and cause the disappearance of this True Dhamma.”
First.

"Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who explain what is an offense as 'not an offense' are acting for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many beings, including devas and humans.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, those bhikkhus generate much demerit and cause the disappearance of this True Dhamma."
The second [case].
"Those monks, bhikkhus, who describe a light offense as a heavy offense... [and so on] ...who describe a heavy offense as a light offense...
[and so on] ...who describe a grave offense as a non-grave offense... [and so on]."

They proclaim a non-gross offense as a gross offense … [and so on] … they proclaim a curable offense as an incurable offense … [and so on] … they proclaim an incurable offense as a curable offense … [and so on] … they proclaim an offense that can be remedied as an offense that cannot be remedied … [and so on] … they proclaim an offense that cannot be remedied as an offense that can be remedied.
“Those monks, bhikkhus, are practicing for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people,
for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many people,
including both gods and humans. Furthermore, bhikkhus, those monks produce much demerit and cause this true Dhamma to disappear.”
The Tenth.

“Those monks, bhikkhus, who explain what is not an offense as ‘not an offense,’ bhikkhus, have set out for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many people, including gods and humans.
Those monks, bhikkhus, produce much merit and establish this true Dhamma.”
Eleventh.

“Those monks, bhikkhus, who point out an offense as ‘an offense,’ are practicing for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many people, including devas and humans.
Those monks, bhikkhus, produce much merit and establish this true Dhamma.”
Twelfth.
“Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who describe a light offense as a light offense...
who describe a grave offense as a grave offense... who describe a gross offense as a gross offense... who describe a non-gross offense as a non-gross offense...”
They explain a non-grave offense as a non-grave offense... they explain an offense with remainder as an offense with remainder...
they explain an offense without remainder as an offense without remainder... they explain an offense remediable by confession as an offense remediable by confession...
they explain an offense not remediable by confession as an offense not remediable by confession.
“Those monks, bhikkhus, have set out for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many people, including gods and humans.
And those monks, bhikkhus, produce much merit; they establish this true Dhamma.
The twentieth [chapter].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.13.
The Chapter on One Person.
“Bhikkhus, one person, arising in the world,
arises for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
What is that one person?”
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

This, monks, is the one person who, arising in the world, arises for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
“Bhikkhus, the manifestation of one person is rare in the world.
Of which one person?
Of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“Indeed, monks, the appearance of this one person in the world is rare.
(AN 1.172, AN 1.13.3, PTS AN i 22) “Monks,
when one person arises in the world, he arises as a marvelous man.”
“Who is that one person?
The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
This, monks, is the one person who, arising in the world, arises as a marvelous man.”
“Bhikkhus, the death of one person is a cause for regret for many people. Which one person? [The answer follows]. (AN 1.173, AN 1.13.4, PTS AN i 22)
“Of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Indeed, monks, the passing away of this one person is a cause for regret for many people.

“Monks, one person, when arising in the world, arises without a second, without a companion, peerless, incomparable, matchless, without rival, unequaled, the equal of the unequaled, the foremost of bipeds.
What is that one person?
The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“Monks, this one person, appearing in the world, appears without a second, without a companion, peerless, incomparable, matchless, without rival, unequaled, equal to the unequaled—
the foremost of bipeds. “Monks, with the manifestation of this one person,
there is the manifestation of great vision, the manifestation of great light.”
There is the manifestation of great radiance; there is the manifestation of the six unsurpassed qualities;
there is the realization of the four analytical knowledges; there is the penetration of the many elements; there is the penetration of the diverse elements;
there is the realization of the fruit of clear knowledge and liberation; there is the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; there is the realization of the fruit of once-returning.

There is the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, there is the realization of the fruit of once-returning, there is the realization of the fruit of non-returning, and there is the realization of the fruit of arhatship.
Of which single person?
Of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
With the manifestation of this one person, monks, there is the manifestation of great vision,
the manifestation of great light, the manifestation of great radiance; there is the manifestation of the six unsurpassed qualities,
the realization of the four analytical knowledges, the penetration of the many elements, and the penetration of the various elements.
"There is the realization of the fruit of clear knowledge and liberation; there is the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; there is the realization of the fruit of once-returning;
there is the realization of the fruit of non-returning; there is the realization of the fruit of arhatship.
“Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single person who rightly continues to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Tathāgata as does Sāriputta.
Sāriputta, bhikkhus, rightly continues to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Tathāgata.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.23 Third Chapter (AN 1.287–295; AN 1.15.20–28; PTS AN i 28) [The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having abandoned the destruction of life, abstaining from the destruction of life, laying aside the rod and the sword, modest, compassionate, and kind to living beings. He dwells having abandoned taking what is not given, abstaining from taking what is not given, taking only what is given, expecting only what is given, being pure in his livelihood. He dwells having abandoned unchastity, living apart, aloof from sexual intercourse, the vulgar practice of common people. He dwells having abandoned false speech, abstaining from false speech, a speaker of truth, one devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, no deceiver of the world. He dwells having abandoned divisive speech, abstaining from divisive speech;

he does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to divide [those people] from these, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere in order to divide [these people] from those; thus he is one who reunites those who are divided, a promoter of unity, who enjoys concord, who delights in concord, a speaker of words that promote concord. He dwells having abandoned harsh speech, abstaining from harsh speech; he speaks whatever is blameless, pleasing to the ear, agreeable to the heart, courteous, desired by many, and agreeable to many. He dwells having abandoned idle chatter, abstaining from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks on the Dhamma and the Vinaya; at the right time he is one who speaks such words as are worth recording, reasonable, moderate, and connected with good. He avoids sitting in private with women, girls, eunuchs, ascetics of other sects, or nuns of other sects. He does not frequent streets, crossroads, marketplaces, royal palaces, or the assemblies of various sectarians. He does not become addicted to alcohol, spirits, and intoxicants which cause heedlessness. He is content with any kind of robe, and he is content with any kind of almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. He dwells restrained according to the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and undertaking and training in the rules of training. He is one who arouses energy for abandoning unwholesome states and for acquiring wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in exertion, not shirking the burden of wholesome qualities. He is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and alertness, one who remembers and recollects what was done and said long ago. He is wise, possessing the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having abandoned the destruction of life... [as above] ...he is wise, possessing the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. But he is not content with any kind of robe, nor is he content with any kind of almsfood, lodging, or medicinal requisites for the sick. He is not one who arouses energy for abandoning unwholesome states and for acquiring wholesome states; he is not steadfast, firm in exertion, but shrinks from the burden of wholesome qualities. He is unmindful, lacking supreme mindfulness and alertness, one who does not remember or recollect what was done and said long ago. He is not wise, not possessing the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. And how, monks, is one a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having abandoned the destruction of life... [as above] ...he is not wise, not possessing the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. And he is not content with any kind of robe, nor is he content with any kind of almsfood, lodging, or medicinal requisites for the sick. He is not one who arouses energy for abandoning unwholesome states and for acquiring wholesome states; he is not steadfast, firm in exertion, but shrinks from the burden of wholesome qualities. He is unmindful, lacking supreme mindfulness and alertness, one who does not remember or recollect what was done and said long ago.
